item.title: ACC starts investigation against Asif Mahmud
item.description:
The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has launched an investigation into former interim government Youth and Sports Adviser Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain and four others over alleged corruption and irregularities in the Ministry of Youth and Sports.
The development was confirmed by ACC sources on Wednesday.
According to media reports, the commission has decided to investigate the involvement of five people, including Asif Mahmud, in alleged corruption and irregularities in the ministry’s activities.
The ACC has formally begun the investigation to verify the allegations, the sources said.

item.title: Disaster authority: Nepal flood toll rises to 1,114 dead, 3,916 missing
item.description:
Devastating floods on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,114 people in Nepal, and 3,916 are missing, the disaster authority said on Wednesday, a week after the disaster.
Chinese state media reported 16 people killed in Tibet and 546 people missing, taking the total toll from the August 26 disaster to 1,130 dead and 4,462 missing.

item.title: Bidisha Ershad denied bail in fraud case
item.description:
The bail application of former president Hussain Muhammad Ershad’s former wife Bidisha Ershad has been rejected in a case filed over alleged fraud in the sale of a flat, meaning she will remain in jail.
Dhaka Bar Association President Anwar Zahid Bhuiyan and several other lawyers appeared for Bidisha before Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge Shahjahan Kabir on Wednesday, seeking bail.
Advocate Hemayet Uddin Khan Hiron, representing the plaintiff, opposed the bail petition.
After the hearing, the court rejected the application, Bidisha’s lawyer Moniruzzaman Sabuj said.
“We sought bail on the condition that she would file an appeal. However, the court rejected the application. We will move the High Court and seek justice there,” he said.
On May 20, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Jamshed Alam sentenced Bidisha to two years in prison and fined her Tk10,000, with an additional month in jail in default.
As Bidisha was absconding, the court issued an arrest warrant and a warrant for her imprisonment.
Police arrested her from a restaurant in Gulshan at around 8:30pm on August 25 based on the warrant. She was produced before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) Court in Dhaka the following day.
Before Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid, her lawyers sought bail on the condition that she would appeal against the conviction. The court rejected the application and ordered her to be sent to jail.
Businessman Mosharraf Hossain Sikder filed the case with Gulshan police station in 2008, alleging fraud in the sale of a flat at President Park in Baridhara.
According to the case statement, Mosharraf was looking to purchase a flat in Baridhara. Through acquaintances, he learned about Bidisha, who showed him a flat at President Park on July 1, 2001, and offered to sell it.
The two parties subsequently reached an agreement to sell the flat for Tk80 lakh, according to the complaint.
The complaint alleges that on July 10, 2001, Bidisha called Mosharraf to the Rajnigandha office in Banani and asked him to provide a Tk75 lakh pay order in the name of her nominee and friend Abdul Razzak.
Mosharraf allegedly paid the amount through Standard Chartered Bank’s Kawran Bazar branch. A memorandum of understanding was subsequently signed between the parties.
Under the agreement, the flat was to be registered after payment of the remaining amount and approval from the Capital Development Authority (Rajuk). However, the plaintiff alleged that the flat was not handed over even after a considerable period, despite being promised by July 10, 2002.
The complaint states that when Mosharraf pressed for the flat to be handed over, Bidisha allegedly promised to return the money.
On February 9, 2005, she allegedly issued a cheque for Tk72 lakh. However, when the cheque was deposited, it was dishonoured due to insufficient funds in the account.
The plaintiff alleged that Bidisha subsequently delayed the matter on various pretexts and failed to return the money or hand over the flat. He also alleged that she threatened to have him killed by hired criminals.

item.title: Funerals in Nepal for missing, a week after deadly floods
item.description:
Nepali families were holding symbolic funeral ceremonies to "liberate the souls" of loved ones missing since deadly flash floods swept away their villages and homes in the Himalayan region a week ago.
Emergency teams have recovered more than 1,000 bodies, and nearly 4,500 people are missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse roared down the China-Nepal border on August 26.
After days of searching shelters and mortuaries, relatives of some of the missing lost hope and began conducting last rites.
"We had to do this to set his soul free, so that he is at peace and happy wherever he is," said Dolma Newar Tamang, flanked by her sobbing son, at a funeral for her husband.
He had been en route to China when the disaster struck.
"I saw the news and called him," she told AFP. "I called repeatedly, but he never picked up."
A week on from the colossal disaster, Nepali rescuers remained hopeful about finding survivors, particularly in multiple tunnels of hydropower plants across the region.
So far, rescuers have recovered only bodies from tunnels blocked by sludge, but teams were still digging, drilling and blasting through debris in the hopes of reaching survivors.
Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said he still hoped some of the thousands missing could be alive.
"Miracles do happen," he told AFP in an interview. "At this point, I do not want to completely give up hope."
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was "a serious indication that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change".
"Climate change is a global contribution, and disaster response is also a global responsibility," he added in a post on Facebook.
Scientists say the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are warming rapidly as global temperatures rise, accelerating glacier melt.
Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.
There is growing anger at the scale of destruction to hit Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people.
The country has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, but is among those suffering its consequences.
Kathmandu has warned reconstruction costs could run into the "billions of dollars".
Nepal's economy is already under pressure, with limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale.
In an illustration of the scale of destruction, Chinese state media said road access to hard-hit Gyirong Port in Tibet had only finally been restored on Wednesday after "days of round-the-clock repair work".
With mortuaries overflowing in Nepal, authorities have had to bury hundreds of unidentified bodies after DNA sampling.
Nepal said 1,050 bodies had been recovered by Tuesday, while 3,916 people remained missing.
China's state media reported 16 dead and 546 missing.
That takes the overall number of reported dead to 1,066 and missing to 4,462.
At least 17 bodies have also been pulled from rivers downstream in India.
In China, foreign journalists are restricted from reporting in Tibet and Chinese authorities have a tight grip on information sources on the region.
Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China's account of the disaster, but Beijing insists that the "release of information has been open, transparent and timely".

item.title: Rain likely across Bangladesh
item.description:
Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) has forecast light to moderate rain across the country in the next 24 hours commencing 9am on Wednesday.
According to the BMD forecast light to moderate rain or thunder showers accompanied by temporary gusty wind is likely to occur at many places over Rangpur, Rajshahi, Dhaka, Mymensingh, Khulna, Barisal, Chittagong and Sylhet divisions.
The Met Office also predicted moderately heavy to heavy falls at places over the country.
Day and night temperatures may remain nearly unchanged across the country, the forecast said.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 11th globally for poor air quality
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 11th among the world’s cities with the worst air quality on Wednesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 105 at 9:35am.
According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups”, poses health risks to children, older adults, and people with heart or lung diseases, while the general public is mostly unaffected.
Kuching in Malaysia topped the global pollution list with an AQI of 346, followed by Kinshasa in the Democratic Republic of Congo with 168 and Kolkata in India with 164.
An AQI reading of 101 to 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, while 151 to 200 is classified as ‘unhealthy’. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered ‘very unhealthy’, and anything above 301 is categorized as ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides a daily indication of air quality by measuring the level of pollution and its potential impact on human health.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants — particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long faced serious air pollution problems, with air quality generally deteriorating during the winter months and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to around 7 million deaths worldwide every year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Can Bangladesh turn its rooftops into power plants?
item.description:
Bangladesh is looking up at the sun because it has run out of convincing answers on the ground. Load shedding has returned with a force that is difficult to ignore. At times, the country has faced an electricity shortfall of several thousand megawatts, leaving households and businesses to endure hours without reliable power.
Against this backdrop, solar energy has acquired an almost irresistible political appeal. If the grid cannot produce enough electricity, perhaps the country’s rooftops can.
The government now wants to increase solar power capacity to 10,000 megawatts during its current term. Its National Renewable Energy Development Strategy 2026-2030 has set an even broader ambition: Renewable energy should account for 20% of total electricity generation by 2030, with rooftop solar alone expected to contribute 5,500 megawatts. These are ambitious numbers. They are also numbers that deserve more scrutiny than applause.
The central idea is simple enough. Bangladesh does not have the luxury of dedicating vast stretches of land to solar parks. Producing one megawatt of solar electricity can require more than two acres, and land is already among the country’s scarcest resources. So instead of searching for empty land, the government wants to use the land it has already built over: Rooftops.
There is something almost poetic about the idea. The roof over a person’s head could also become a small power station. A factory could produce both garments and electricity. A shopping centre could become a generator. Millions of ordinary buildings could collectively become a giant distributed power plant. Through net metering, consumers could use the electricity they generate and send their surplus to the national grid.
But poetry does not pay for solar panels.
A three-kilowatt rooftop solar system can cost around Tk 3 lakh. The investment may potentially be recovered over five or six years, depending on electricity generation, loan costs, roof size, and equipment quality. For a middle-class household, however, Tk 3 lakh is not an insignificant amount. For millions of families and small businesses, it is the difference between an attractive energy solution and an impossible purchase.
That is why financing will determine whether Bangladesh’s rooftop solar dream becomes a mass movement or remains a program for those who already have money. Experts estimate that generating 500 megawatts through rooftop solar could require panels on roughly 10 to 12 lakh rooftops and an investment of Tk 30,000-40,000 crore. The question is not simply whether such money exists. The question is whether ordinary people and small entrepreneurs can actually access it.
The government has discussed low-interest loans, tax and customs benefits, start-up funds, and installment facilities. All of these sound encouraging. But Bangladesh has never suffered from a shortage of promising financial schemes on paper. The real test begins when a small entrepreneur walks into a bank and asks for money.
There is another danger. A program intended to democratize energy could end up creating another concentrated market. The government says young people, women, and small and medium entrepreneurs will be encouraged to participate through local service providers. But without adequate finance, training, and institutional support, the smaller players could become little more than subcontractors for large companies.
The technical challenge is equally serious. A rooftop solar system is not something that can simply be installed, photographed, and forgotten. Panels, inverters, and other equipment require maintenance. Faulty installations can reduce efficiency or become expensive burdens for consumers. If millions of rooftops are to become part of the electricity system, Bangladesh will need a large network of properly trained technicians capable of maintaining them over years, not merely installing them in the first place.
This is where the government’s proposed service-provider model could either succeed brilliantly or become another bureaucratic experiment. Area-based companies are expected to provide technical assistance, financing and business packages, customer service, installation and maintenance. The model makes sense. But it immediately raises another question: Who will watch the service providers?
A consumer who receives poor mobile service can change operators. Someone whose rooftop solar system fails after installation may not have such an easy escape. The regulatory system must therefore be designed before the market becomes crowded.
The most uncomfortable issue, however, may be institutional accountability. The renewable energy sector already involves several state agencies, and questions have been raised about who will ultimately regulate, supervise, and implement the new initiative. If the same institutional structure becomes simultaneously policy-maker, participant, and supervisor, accountability can quickly become a circular exercise in which everyone is responsible and nobody is accountable.
That is particularly dangerous in Bangladesh’s energy sector, where large sums of public and private money are involved. Solar power should not become another arena in which ambitious targets are celebrated while the details of procurement, pricing, quality control, and enforcement remain obscure.
Then comes the question that could determine the entire economics of rooftop solar: What is the electricity actually worth?
Net metering works because consumers have an incentive to generate electricity and send excess power into the grid. But that incentive depends on the price at which surplus electricity is valued. Set the price too low and consumers will not find the investment attractive. Set it too high and the cost could eventually be transferred to the power sector and, ultimately, the public.
A transparent benchmark price is therefore the economic foundation of the entire program. Investors need predictability. Consumers need to know when their investment will pay back. Banks need to calculate risk. Regulators need to understand the fiscal consequences. Without a credible pricing model, everyone is being asked to invest in a market whose rules are still moving.
Bangladesh’s previous experience should also make policy-makers cautious. More than six million solar home systems were distributed in rural areas beginning in 2003, demonstrating that the country can adopt solar technology on a large scale. But moving from off-grid systems to millions of grid-connected rooftop systems is a much more complicated proposition. It requires not only panels but a grid capable of absorbing electricity generated by thousands or millions of independent producers.
There is also little wisdom in making solar mandatory simply because the government wants the numbers to rise quickly. A previous requirement for rooftop solar on certain multi-storey buildings has reportedly produced limited results. That should tell policy-makers something important: People do not necessarily resist solar energy; they resist systems that make them pay without giving them reliable service, predictable savings, or adequate support.
The smarter approach is to make solar economically irresistible rather than administratively compulsory. If grid electricity becomes increasingly expensive and rooftop generation genuinely lowers monthly costs, consumers will not need much persuasion. They will install panels because the mathematics tells them to.
The government’s solar ambition, therefore, should not be judged by how many megawatts it announces. It should be judged by what happens after the panels are installed.
There are several questions that need to be answered:
Do they continue working five years later? Can consumers obtain affordable financing? Are technicians available outside Dhaka? Can a small entrepreneur compete with a large corporation? Is the price of surplus electricity transparent? Can a consumer complain when a service provider fails? Can regulators punish negligence without political or commercial interference?
These questions are less glamorous than announcing 10,000 megawatts but they are the questions that will determine whether those megawatts ever become meaningful.
Bangladesh’s energy crisis has created a powerful case for renewable energy. The country cannot continue treating imported fuel, expensive generation, and recurring load shedding as permanent features of economic life. Solar power offers an opportunity to diversify the energy system while creating new businesses, jobs and local investment.
But sunlight alone cannot solve an institutional problem.
Bangladesh may have millions of roofs and plenty of sunlight, but neither resource will automatically produce reliable electricity. What will matter is whether the government can build a system in which money is accessible, prices are fair, equipment is reliable, technicians are competent, regulators are independent, and service providers are accountable.
The country is ready to put solar panels on its rooftops. The bigger question is whether its institutions are ready to stand underneath them.
HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Promises must be kept regarding the gas crisis
item.description:
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi has assured the public that normal gas supply will be restored by the first or second week of September. After what appears to be several weeks of severe shortages, factory disruptions, and household frustration, this is a commitment that demands scrutiny -- and follow‑through.
We are no strangers to repeated assurances about energy stabilization in the past, only to see the crisis persist. This time, the government must be held to its word.
While the crisis has rightfully been attributed to global instability, pointing to the US-Israel attack on Iran and the subsequent conflict and disruptions in shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, there is no denying that Bangladesh has not planned well when it comes to diversifying its energy sources.
Bangladesh’s domestic energy failures are a result of more than just global events, and the public deserves clarity, not deflection when it comes to them. The crisis has already caused widespread hardship, and citizens need solutions, not geopolitical narratives.
While Prime Minister Tarique Rahman allocating Tk40,000 crore to the energy and power sector to address the shortage is certainly a significant sum, it is meaningless if it does not translate into measurable improvements. Bangladesh has seen large allocations before, but without transparent implementation, spending alone does not guarantee relief.
The real test here is simple: Will households and industries actually experience the normalization promised by September?
Bangladesh cannot afford another cycle of promises without action. The gas and power crisis has undermined industrial output, strained household budgets, and weakened public confidence.
The government must deliver tangible results, and will be judged by whether gas actually flows again, not by statements made at press briefings.

item.title: A worrying sign for human rights
item.description:
The latest monthly review from the Manabadhikar Shongskriti Foundation (MSF) should compel our nation and its leaders to pause, and must be heeded as a warning that Bangladesh’s human rights situation is potentially deteriorating across multiple fronts, and fast.
The sheer scale of the increases documented in August should force a national reckoning.
Start with the most vulnerable: Killings of women and children jumped 75%, rising from 52 in July to 91 in August. Violence against women and children climbed to 327 incidents, gang rape rose 72%, rape‑and‑murder cases surged 67%, and suicides increased 39%.
While month to month numbers should be taken with a pinch of salt, the absolute numbers still are signs of a society struggling to protect its most basic rights.
Political violence also spiked sharply. Injuries soared 181%, from 95 to 267, even as deaths dipped slightly. The violence involved activists from across the political spectrum -- BNP, NCP, Jamaat, Awami League -- showing that no party can claim innocence.
Most alarming, however, is the rise in attacks on minority communities. MSF documented 26 incidents in August, more than triple the eight recorded in July. Idol vandalism, threats, and assaults paint a picture of communities living in fear while the state struggles to respond.
Bangladesh cannot afford complacency. These statistics reflect real people, real suffering, and real failures of protection that citizens of this country have every right to expect.
The state must respond, whether that be through stronger rule of law, credible investigations, or just reassuring the people that they are aware of the situation.
Moreover, every government owes its people unwavering commitment to safeguarding every citizen -- especially those most at risk.

item.title: A closed road, an open question
item.description:
One morning recently, I was travelling by car and was supposed to be dropped off at Sonargaon. The usual route from Hatirjheel towards Kawran Bazar, however, was closed. The driver had to take an alternative route before reaching Sonargaon.
The journey became much longer than expected. Nearly an hour was lost.
As I watched the traffic crawl along an unfamiliar route, I realized that the road closure and resulting congestion were certainly real problems. But so was our tendency to react to such disruptions with disproportionate frustration and anger. The inconvenience is real; our response can sometimes make it worse.
A driver becomes angry because another car has stopped for a few seconds. A motorcyclist shouts at a pedestrian. A pedestrian responds angrily to a driver. Someone honks repeatedly because traffic is not moving, as if the sound of the horn could somehow make the road wider. At a shop, government office, hospital, queue or on public transport, people often seem to be operating with very little patience.
Sometimes, even a small disruption is enough to push us over the edge. Why?
Perhaps because we have become accustomed to living with uncertainty and inconvenience. Traffic congestion, road construction, power interruptions, bureaucratic delays, crowded public spaces, and unreliable services are part of everyday life. We plan our day knowing that something may go wrong. Yet instead of becoming more tolerant of disruptions, we often seem to have developed shorter tempers.
The irony is that we already know things frequently do not go according to plan. Yet when something actually goes wrong, we react as though it should never have happened.
The closed road that morning was beyond my control. I could not reopen the crossing, remove the traffic, or recover the lost hour. I could either spend the journey becoming increasingly frustrated or accept the situation and ask a more useful question: What can I do now?
That distinction matters.
When something goes wrong, our first instinct is often to look for someone to blame. But blame does not necessarily solve the immediate problem. Nor does anger.
There is an important difference between reacting to a problem and responding to it.
Reaction is immediate. Response requires a pause.
Reaction asks, “Why is this happening?” Response asks, “What can I do now?”
This does not mean that we should accept poor services, bad planning, or inefficient systems without question. We should demand better roads, better traffic management, better public services, and greater accountability. But there is a difference between addressing a systemic problem and dealing with an immediate inconvenience.
A person stuck in traffic cannot solve Dhaka's transportation crisis from behind the steering wheel. A passenger who is already late cannot recover the lost hour by becoming angry. And aggressive driving will not make a closed road reopen.
Yet our streets are full of precisely this kind of frustration.
More worrying is how quickly irritation spreads. One person's impatience can become another person's aggression. A honk becomes an insult; an insult becomes an argument; an argument can become a confrontation. A minor inconvenience that could have ended in seconds can turn into a much bigger conflict.
Perhaps we need to pay greater attention to something very ordinary: Civility.
Small courtesies do not solve structural problems, but they make everyday life more manageable. A simple “thank you” or an apology, allowing someone to pass or responding calmly when someone makes a mistake, can prevent unnecessary conflict.
Yet these basic gestures increasingly seem to be disappearing from public life.
An apology can be seen as weakness. Allowing someone to go ahead can feel like losing. Even acknowledging the service of a driver, security guard, shopkeeper, or other worker can sometimes seem unnecessary.
But societies are not held together only by laws and institutions. They are also shaped by thousands of everyday interactions between strangers.
The way we speak to one another matters. So does the way we behave when we are inconvenienced.
That last point may be particularly important. It is easy to be polite when everything is going according to plan. The real test comes when we are late, stuck, tired, frustrated, or inconvenienced.
We cannot control every road closure or traffic jam. We cannot control every mistake made by another person. But we can decide whether to add another layer of anger to an already difficult situation.
This is not an argument for passivity. We should continue to question poor planning, demand accountability, and push for better systems. But while those larger problems are being addressed, we still have to navigate the daily realities in front of us.
Perhaps that is the lesson from a closed road. Sometimes the practical response is simply to find another route.
Perhaps Bangladesh needs better roads and better traffic management. But we also need better habits of dealing with one another: Less aggression, more patience, and a little more civility in everyday life.
Because when everyone is already losing time, there is little reason to make one another lose our peace as well.
Nazmun Naher is a water resources expert with extensive experience in regional and international integrated water resources management. She can be reached at nnazmun.mita@gmail.com.

item.title: Father, two sons found dead in Jessore home
item.description:
The bodies of a man and his two sons were recovered from their home in Sharsha upazila of Jessore on Tuesday afternoon.
The deceased were identified as Kamal Hossain, 45, and his sons Sabir, 5, and Jabir, around two and a half years old.
Sharsha police station Officer-in-Charge Shaminul Haque confirmed the incident.
He said that they initially suspect Kamal killed his two sons by strangulation before taking his own life.
“The investigation will determine how the children died and the exact circumstances of the incident,” the OC added.
According to local sources, Kamal had seven children from multiple marriages. He had divorced his first two wives. His latest wife reportedly left for her parents’ home in Narail about a week ago following a family dispute, leaving the two children with their father.

item.title: Germany defender Rudiger announces international retirement
item.description:
Germany defender Antonio Rudiger on Tuesday announced his international retirement, two months after last playing for Germany at the 2026 World Cup.
The 33-year-old made 86 appearances for the four-time world champions.
"After some time reflecting, the moment has come for me to end my national team career and clear the way for the young generation," Rudiger said in a social media post.
Rudiger made his debut in 2014, a month before Germany won the World Cup, but was not included in the squad which travelled to Brazil.
The centre-back said he wanted to focus on his club side Real Madrid, where he is under contract until 2027.

item.title: BCB charges three over alleged BPL anti-corruption breaches
item.description:
The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) has charged three individuals with alleged breaches of the anti-corruption code in connection with the 12th edition of the Bangladesh Premier League (BPL), the board said in a statement on Tuesday.
The three accused are former BCB director and former chairman of the board's audit committee Muhammad Mukhlesur Rahman Shamim, former BCB security liaison officer (SLO) Zakir Hossain, and former BCB councillor for Bogra district and former audit committee member secretary Rakibul Islam Sunny.
The charges followed an investigation by the BCB's Integrity Unit into alleged violations of various provisions of the ICC Anti-Corruption Code for Participants 2024.
The allegations include attempting to influence the result, progress or other aspects of a BPL match, encouraging or assisting a participant to engage in corrupt conduct, failing to report corrupt approaches or communications in a timely manner, failing to cooperate with an investigation and obstructing or delaying an investigation.
Shamim has been charged under Articles 2.1.1, 2.1.4, 2.4.4 and 2.4.7. The allegations include attempting to influence the outcome or progress of a match, encouraging or assisting another participant in corrupt activity, failing to report a corrupt offer to the Anti-Corruption Officer and obstructing an investigation by concealing, deleting or destroying relevant communications or information.
Zakir has been charged under Articles 2.1.1, 2.1.4 and 2.4.6. He is accused of attempting to influence the outcome or other aspects of a match through irregular means, encouraging or assisting a participant in corrupt activity and failing to cooperate with the investigation.
Sunny faces charges under Articles 2.4.4 and 2.4.6. He is accused of failing to report information relating to a proposal to engage in corrupt conduct in a timely manner and failing to cooperate with the investigation.
The BCB said all three individuals have been provisionally suspended. They will have 14 days from receiving the notices of charge to respond to the allegations, after which disciplinary proceedings will be conducted in accordance with the anti-corruption code.
The board said it would not make any further comment on the matter at this stage.The charges are allegations and do not represent a final finding of wrongdoing. Any disciplinary outcome will follow the prescribed proceedings under the code.

item.title: Cricketers to get best rooms at Asian Games, says Japan chief
item.description:
Cricketers at this month's Asian Games in Japan will have better accommodation than athletes from many other sports, the head of Japanese cricket said Wednesday, after concerns were raised about a lack of five-star hotels for players.
A Sri Lankan official said this week that some of Asia's top teams had raised doubts over facilities and accommodation at the Games, which are taking place in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from September 19.
Cricket is a minor sport in Japan and games will be played at a new purpose-built ground with reports of tents serving as dressing rooms and distant washroom facilities.
There is no dedicated athletes' village at the Games, with organisers instead relying on cabins in a cruise ship, rooms in temporary wooden containers and hotels.
Organisers said last week that accommodation was already stretched to the limit after the number of Asian Games athletes ballooned to 17,000.
By comparison there were around 11,000 at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
The cricket tournament is being run by the Asian Games organising committee in collaboration with the Asian Cricket Council (ACC).
Naoki Alex Miyaji, the CEO of the Japan Cricket Association, told AFP that the two bodies had been discussing accommodation options "for a long time".
"The participating teams in cricket are being offered hotel accommodation," Miyaji said on Wednesday.
"Many other sports are being accommodated in much more limited facilities such as a cruise ship or container hotels."
Matches will be played at Korogi Sports Park, a converted baseball field that is a 40-minute train ride away from central Nagoya.
Media reports in India said the country's cricket board was unhappy with arrangements and might send a second-string squad after originally naming 15 players led by Shreyas Iyer and including 15-year-old rising star Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
Miyaji said that Japanese organisers "only had 17 months to prepare and had to start from scratch" for cricket at the Games.
He said they had been working "to ensure that the best facilities are provided within the limited timeline and facility restrictions".
"Despite being temporary, the facilities will provide as comfortable a space as possible for the players and officials," he said.
Miyaji said the pitch, which is being prepared by the curator of the 35,000-capacity Pallekele International Cricket Stadium in Sri Lanka, would be of a high standard.
"From what I have seen, the playing surface and field will be the best seen in cricket's inclusion in the Asian Games," he added.

item.title: Court documents: Tiger Woods set to change not guilty plea in DUI case
item.description:
Tiger Woods, who pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence after crashing his car in Florida in March, is expected to formally change his plea, court documents showed Tuesday.
A "change of plea" hearing early Wednesday morning was added to the golf superstar's case docket at a Martin County court, online records showed.
Woods' lawyer did not immediately respond to AFP request for comment about the nature of the change of plea.
The 15-time major winner crashed his SUV into a trailer being pulled by a pickup truck near his Jupiter Island home in March.
He was assessed to be impaired by officers at the scene, and had opioid painkillers with him.
Woods pleaded not guilty to misdemeanor charges of DUI with property damage and refusing to submit to a lawful test, telling authorities he was looking at his phone and changing radio channels when he crashed.
Days later he said he was "stepping away" to seek treatment and focus on his health.
He was cleared by a judge to travel overseas to an inpatient facility, reportedly in Switzerland.
Woods made his first public appearance since his arrest at the PGA Tour's Travelers Championship in June.
The following month, a judge ruled that prosecutors could review Woods' hospital treatment, as well as the golfer's prescription drug records.
In both cases the information can be reviewed only by prosecutors and designated law enforcement officers and experts and Woods's defense team.
Woods has undergone multiple back operations and surgeries on severe leg injuries suffered in a separate, 2021 California car crash.

item.title: Man City sign Fernandez, Ndiaye as Premier League clubs set new spending record
item.description:
Premier League clubs shattered their record of £3.1 billion ($4.2 billion) in transfer fees in one window on deadline day as Manchester City splashed out £125 million to Chelsea for Enzo Fernandez and signed Iliman Ndiaye.
City spearheaded a frantic final day of spending as they aim to arm Enzo Maresca with a squad capable of winning the Premier League for the first time in three seasons.
Fernandez, who previously thrived under Maresca at Chelsea, has been linked with a move to the Etihad for months.
But it took until the final hours before the 2200 GMT deadline for an agreement to be reportedly struck with the fee for the Argentine to match the British transfer record that Liverpool paid for Alexander Isak on the final day of the window last year.
Fernandez will form a completely revamped City midfield alongside England international Elliot Anderson and Moroccan Ayyoub Bouaddi, who themselves cost over a combined £200 million.
"He is a complete midfielder: technically gifted, hardworking, tenacious and a goalscorer," said City's director of football Hugo Viana.
City also added Senegal forward Ndiaye from Everton in a deal worth £65 million to bolster their forward options.
"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye.
"To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."
Chelsea's bid to replace Fernandez with Monaco's Lamine Camara collapsed when the French side reportedly pulled out of the deal.
The Blues did agree a £40 million deal to sign 18-year-old Honest Ahanor from Atalanta from 2027, with the Italy defender spending this season on loan at Crystal Palace.
Champions Arsenal, by contrast, had a quiet deadline day after their pursuit of Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez fizzled out.
The Gunners had been rivalling Barcelona for the Argentine's signature, but the Spanish champions instead turned to Arsenal to fill their need for a forward with the signing of Gabriel Jesus.
"I had a chance 10 years ago and life took me in another direction, but now I can be here and it's a dream for me," said Jesus.
- Liverpool frustrated -
Liverpool splashed out on France forward Bradley Barcola on Monday, spending £123 million to lure him from Paris Saint-Germain.
But the Reds' attempts to further add to their squad look to have been frustrated with bids for Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr and Brighton's Yankuba Minteh knocked back, meaning Cody Gakpo is set to stay despite interest from City and Tottenham.
Liverpool did complete the signing of Belgian goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans, but the 18-year-old will be loaned back to Genk for the rest of the season.
Ibrahim Mbaye was another wide player linked with a move to Anfield, but he has instead joined Aston Villa for a reported £47 million.
Mbaye played 31 times in all competitions for PSG last season as the French club won the Champions League and the Ligue 1 title.
Villa also bolstered their defence by signing Southampton centre-back Taylor Harwood-Bellis in a £29 million deal.
Tottenham secured a loan move for Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk after missing out on Ndiaye and Gakpo, and a £7 million swoop for his Blues team-mate Tosin Adarabioyo.
Jack Grealish rejoined Everton on loan after his spell with David Moyes's men last season.
Everton are still hopeful of adding United States international Folarin Balogun from Monaco.
Newcastle landed Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille in a £51 million swoop.
The Magpies, who are rebuilding following the close-season departures of Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali, have also sent German striker Nicolas Woltemade on loan to Juventus.

item.title: After triple century, Hridoy breaks Tamim’s 334-run record
item.description:
Towhid Hridoy is breaking record after record. His triple century against South Africa A in Potchefstroom had already secured his place in history. He became the first Bangladeshi batter to score a triple century on foreign soil.

Now Hridoy has added another record to his name. Until today, Tamim Iqbal held the record for the highest individual score by a Bangladeshi batter in first-class cricket, with 334 runs. He achieved the feat for East Zone against Central Zone in Mirpur during the 2019 Bangladesh Cricket League (BCL).

Towhid Hridoy becomes first Bangladeshi to score triple century abroad

Hridoy surpassed that record in South Africa. Bangladesh A declared their innings with Hridoy unbeaten on 350.

Play ended yesterday after Saifuddin was dismissed. Bangladesh A resumed the final day with four wickets in hand but lost two early in the morning. When the eighth wicket fell, Hridoy was on 225.

From there, Rezaur Rahman gave him excellent support. Hridoy carried the innings through to the declaration alongside Rezaur. Bangladesh A declared at 676 for eight in the first innings, with Hridoy unbeaten on 350 off 481 balls and Rezaur unbeaten on 31 off 110 balls.

South Africa A began their second innings 164 runs behind. However, Bangladesh still have little chance of winning, as the bowlers have less than a full session remaining to bowl South Africa A out.

item.title: Gunfire in Gendaria: Who is behind the fight for drugs, dominance?
item.description:
A violent struggle for control of the drug trade, extortion and territorial influence along Gendaria’s railway corridor has emerged as the driving force behind Sunday night’s gunfight in Swamibagh Munsirtek, where rival groups turned a narrow residential alley into a battleground and left three bystanders shot.
At the centre of the conflict are two competing networks, one linked by police and locals to jailed alleged drug dealer “Auto Sajal” and the other to local BNP leader Md Monir Hossain.
Monir’s personal office. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Police and local sources said the groups have been locked in a long-running dispute over control of the drug trade and dominance around the Gendaria railway line.
Both sides face allegations of involvement in illegal firearms, drugs, extortion and other criminal activities.
Dhaka Tribune visited Munsirtek on Tuesday, spoke to witnesses and residents and reviewed CCTV footage and police information to reconstruct what led to the gunfight.
Two days after the violence, fear remained palpable. Some shops were closed, while residents were reluctant to discuss what they had witnessed.
According to residents, Sajal had long maintained influence over the drug trade along the railway corridor, with one local resident claiming his network stretched from Sayedabad to Kamalapur.
But the balance began changing after August 2024, locals alleged, as Monir’s followers increasingly sought control over drugs and extortion in parts of the area.
The rivalry intensified after police arrested Sajal and eight associates with six firearms during a raid in Sayedabad on June 18. They remain in jail.
Some residents alleged that Sajal’s imprisonment created an opening for Monir to expand his network and seek greater control of the area.
They also claimed his interest in contesting for councillor in the upcoming local government elections was connected to his attempts to strengthen his local influence.
Monir, however, rejected allegations that he was attempting to take control of the drug trade or extortion.
The immediate confrontation began earlier on Sunday.
According to multiple witnesses, CCTV footage and police information, Monir and his followers allegedly went to the home of Auto Sajal’s father, Alam, and uncle Russell and assaulted them.
Later that afternoon, Monir’s followers detained three youths -- Rakib, Billal and Rifat -- near the Gendaria railway line on allegations of selling drugs.
The three were taken to Monir’s office, allegedly beaten and subsequently handed over to police.
Police said 96 yaba pills and 30-35 packets of marijuana were recovered from them.
Shortly after police left, a group of around 25-30 people entered Munsirtek Street from the Karatitola end and attacked Monir’s office.
Current view of BNP leader Monir’s personal office. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Gunfire erupted, shops were vandalised and the two sides chased each other through the neighbourhood.
“The intensity of the shooting was so high that it was not clear who was doing it or from which direction,” shopkeeper Idris Mia told Dhaka Tribune.
Some shopkeepers managed to pull down their shutters, while others fled, leaving their shops open.
Electricity also went out during the attack, plunging the alley into darkness and intensifying the panic.
Police said Monir himself fired a pistol during the confrontation and that the firearm was unlicensed.
Police recovered 20 spent bullet casings and one intact bullet from the scene.
Bullet-riddled shutter, a CID evidence item. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The fight for influence also has a political dimension.
A section of local BNP leaders and activists alleged that former councillor and Gendaria Thana BNP President Maqbool Islam Tipu considers both Monir and Auto Sajal rivals.
Local residents had earlier submitted complaints to the DMP commissioner alleging drugs, extortion and criminal activities involving Tipu, while allegations have also been made that Sajal operated his drug business under Tipu’s protection.
These claims have not been independently established.
Tipu rejected the allegations and instead accused Monir of attempting to establish himself locally, engage in extortion and obtain “benefits” from the administration.
Photo of the shop owned by shooting victim Alamgir. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
He acknowledged that some of Sajal’s followers were associated with juvenile gangs and the drug trade along the railway line, but criticised the alleged assault on Sajal’s father.
Monir offered a different account.
He said he had taken the initiative to catch three drug dealers and hand them over to police, prompting people involved in the drug trade to attack his office.
He claimed to have identified Sajal’s father and nephew among the attackers.
Caught between the competing groups were people with no apparent connection to their rivalry.
Siam, 18, had come to Swamibagh to help take his sick aunt to a doctor.
He was sitting at his uncle’s shop when the shooting began.
“Suddenly, many people were coming screaming,” he said.
As they tried to shut the shop, a bullet pierced the shutter and struck his right shoulder.
Tea seller Alamgir, 33, was shot in the forehead before he could close his shop and later underwent surgery.
Asha Akter, 20, was also shot, with an X-ray showing a bullet lodged in her waist. Doctors were preparing to remove it.
Investigators are now trying to determine where the firearms used in the clash came from.
Intelligence sources said preliminary findings raised suspicion that weapons looted from police during the August 2024 unrest may have been used.
However, police stressed that this has not been confirmed.
“We are not sure whether the shooting was done with the looted weapons or not. The matter will be clear once the weapons are recovered,” DMP Wari Division Deputy Commissioner Mallik Ahsan Uddin Sami said.
He was clearer about the underlying cause: “The issue of the shooting is definitely based on dominance.”
Despite three people being shot and firearms being used openly, no case had been filed at Gendaria Police Station as of Tuesday.
Police said CCTV footage from several locations was being analysed, with at least five or six people seen participating in the clash being identified and their roles verified.
For residents of Munsirtek, however, the consequences of the fight for control are already visible.
Two days after the bullets stopped, the alley remained subdued, shops partly shuttered and residents reluctant to speak about the rival networks operating around them.

item.title: Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as ‘Trump Strait’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as “Trump Strait” despite the fact that the crucial waterway remains contested amid the war with Iran.
“Now that we have it under USA. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump said on his Truth Social network.
It is the latest geographical name change floated by Trump and comes a week after he ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as “Lake America” amid a trade war with Canada.
Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” on his first day back in office in January 2025.
Neither Mexico nor Canada have accepted the changes.
Many of the previous name changes started off as apparently jovial remarks by the 80-year-old US president before he then followed through to make them a reality.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly pressed a threat to claim sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, even posting a map showing the waterway as a “new US territory.”
But Iran has effectively shut down the chokepoint, through which a fifth of the world’s oil passes, in retaliation for the war Trump started along with Israel in late February.
Oil prices are rising again after US forces launched fresh strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in response to what Trump said were new minelaying efforts by Iran.

item.title: Man to die for killing Rangpur journalist
item.description:
A Rangpur court on Wednesday sentenced a man to death and two others to life imprisonment for killing journalist Mashiur Rahman alias Utshya Rahman in 2015.
Rangpur District and Sessions Judge Mashiur Rahman handed down the punishment.
The condemned convict is Rubel alias Hekram, while the two convicts sentenced to life imprisonment are Alin and Shubho Kumar. All three were tried in absentia.
The court also acquitted three people including Johiron Akter Jui, an alleged drug peddler and the alleged mastermind of the killing, as the charges brought against them could not be proved.
According to the prosecution, journalist Mashiur Rahman alias Utshya Rahman of the Dainik Juger Alo went missing on December 23, 2015, after leaving his home for work.
Later, his body was recovered from Dharma Das in Rangpur city, with his hands and legs tied to a tree.
Nurjahan Begum Nuri, mother of Mashiur, filed a case with Kotwali Police Station.
Police later submitted a charge sheet against eight people, while the court framed charges against six accused in the case.

item.title: Rangamati hanging bridge submerged as Kaptai Lake water rises
item.description:
Rangamati’s iconic hanging bridge has been submerged as the water level of Kaptai Lake rose sharply following days of heavy rain and upstream runoff from the hills.
The popular tourist attraction is now off-limits to visitors, leaving hundreds of tourists disappointed and dealing a blow to the local tourism industry.
The Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation has suspended access to the bridge for safety reasons. Red flags have been placed at the entrance and bamboo barriers installed to prevent visitors from entering the submerged structure.
Tourists arriving from different parts of the country said they were disappointed after finding the bridge underwater.
“I had wanted to see Rangamati’s Hanging Bridge up close for a long time. But after coming here, I found that the bridge was submerged. I could not even take a picture. It was really disappointing,” said Mohammad Ashraful Islam, who travelled from Dhaka with his family.
The closure has also affected businesses that depend on tourist arrivals.
More than a hundred engine-powered boats are reportedly lying idle at the local boat terminal as tourists have stopped coming for trips on Kaptai Lake.
Shops selling traditional clothing, textiles and handicrafts are also struggling due to the sharp decline in customers, with some traders saying their daily sales have fallen to almost zero.
Mohammad Fakhrul Islam, leaseholder of the local Boat Owners’ Association, said the current period is crucial for their livelihoods.
“The tourist rush during this time of year helps support our families throughout the year. But since the bridge was submerged, our income has completely stopped. If the situation continues, we will have to bear significant financial losses,” he said.
Hotel owner Mohammad Sumon Mia said the hanging bridge is one of the main attractions for visitors to Rangamati.
“Many tourists come to Rangamati to visit the bridge. Since it was submerged, hotel bookings have been cancelled every day. The decline in tourist arrivals is causing losses for hotels, motels and restaurants,” he said.
Alok Bikash Chakma, manager of Rangamati Tourism Corporation, said the bridge was submerged after the water level of Kaptai Lake rose due to heavy rainfall and runoff from the hills.
“The bridge is currently under 4-6 inches of water. For the safety of visitors, we have put up red flags and blocked access with bamboo barriers,” he said.
He said authorities hope the water level will recede within a few days, after which the restrictions on visitors will be lifted.
Meanwhile, Rangamati District Council Chairman Dipan Talukdar Dipu said a survey for the construction of a new bridge had already been conducted.
“We hope construction of a new, modern bridge at a higher elevation will begin soon. Once completed, the new bridge will help attract more tourists to Rangamati,” he said.

item.description:
Heavy rain triggered severe waterlogging in several parts of Rajshahi city and Chapainawabganj town causing widespread suffering for residents and disrupting normal movement.
The Rajshahi Weather Office recorded 99.4 millimetres of rainfall on Wednesday morning, the highest rainfall recorded in the city this season.
Several major roads and lanes were inundated, including areas in front of the Divisional Commissioner’s Office and Rajshahi Medical College Hospital, as well as Barnali intersection, Hetemkha and Laxmipur. In some areas, knee-deep water covered the roads.
Motorcycles and auto-rickshaws became stranded in the water, while office-goers, students and pedestrians struggled to move through the flooded streets. The situation caused traffic disruptions and made it difficult for people to reach their workplaces, educational institutions and other destinations.
Although the water began to recede after the rain stopped, normal movement remained disrupted throughout the morning.
Anwar Hossain, a resident of the Barnali intersection area, said even a short spell of rain often leaves roads flooded.
“Rajshahi is known as one of the country’s cleanest and most beautiful cities, but even a little rain causes waterlogging, making it difficult to move around. The drains are not cleaned regularly, which makes the problem worse,” he said.
College student Anika Tabassum said waterlogging frequently creates problems for students.
“Even moderate rain makes it difficult to attend classes. Road water often mixes with waste from the drains, creating an unbearable stench,” she said.
The latest downpour has once again exposed Rajshahi’s persistent waterlogging problem, leaving residents to suffer from flooded roads, traffic disruption and foul-smelling stagnant water.
Mostafa Kamal Hossain, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension in Rajshahi, also said rainfall at this stage creates favourable conditions for better growth and yield of Aman rice. He said adequate water is particularly important during the flowering and grain-forming stages of the crop for achieving a good yield.
Rainwater has entered homes, government offices, educational institutions, student hostels and other establishments in Chapainawabganj town. Several roads have been submerged under ankle-deep water, while water has risen to knee level in some areas.
Light rain began on Tuesday evening before turning into heavy downpours around midnight. As a result, several areas of the municipality, including Arambagh, Shantir Mor, Batenkhan’s Mor, Old Market, New Market and Udayan Mor, have been flooded.
Several roads have become nearly impassable due to the waterlogging. In some areas, residents have been temporarily confined to their homes as water accumulated in front of their houses. Parts of kitchens and tube-wells have also gone underwater, while water has entered several student hostels.
Local residents blamed inadequate drainage facilities, poor maintenance of existing drains and unplanned urbanisation for the recurring waterlogging in the municipality. They said even moderate rainfall often causes several areas to become flooded.
Safi, a resident of Arambagh, said, “Even when there was heavy rain in the past, water never entered our homes. This time, our houses have been flooded. We are struggling to protect our belongings. We urge the municipal authorities to take immediate measures to address the problem.”

State Minister Yasser: Govt not controlling media in any way
item.description:
The government is not controlling any media outlet, and the media are enjoying more freedom than at any time in the past, State Minister for Information and Broadcasting Yasser Khan Choudhury told Parliament on Wednesday.
“Following Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s instructions, we do not want to control the media in any way, and we are not doing so,” he said, while replying to a supplementary question from National Citizen Party (NCP) lawmaker Abdul Hannan Masud (Noakhali-6) during the question-answer session in Parliament.
The state minister responded to the questions in the absence of Information and Broadcasting Minister Andaleeve Rahman in the House.
He said the media are independent and it is entirely up to any media outlet to decide which news they will upload, remove, publish or not publish. “The Bangladesh government does not interfere in this matter,” he said.
“If a media outlet realises after publishing a report that the information is incorrect or that the report should not have been published, it can remove the report. We do not interfere in such matters. We believe in press freedom, and that is why we will not interfere,” Yasser said.
Earlier, in his supplementary question, Hannan Masud alleged that some news reports critical of the government or its ministers have been removed from media outlets or have become inaccessible following publication.
He said the removal of the news reports has raised questions in the public mind about whether the government is stifling freedom of expression.
The lawmaker sought an explanation from the information and broadcasting minister on this matter.
In reply to another supplementary question from independent lawmaker Sultana Jesmen (Women Seat-49), the state minister said many journalists with political ideologies are members of press clubs, which is a normal process.
“Anyone can have their own political views or ideology. But we expect them to play a neutral role in journalism,” he said.
Yasser said the ministry is working to check misinformation, disinformation, untrue and fake information circulating on social media through various fact-checking initiatives.
Responding to a question from ruling party lawmaker SM Jahangir Alam (Dhaka-18), the information and broadcasting minister said the Press Council Act does not provide for trying a person merely on the basis of a complaint. “If a complaint is proved, the Press Council can only issue a warning, reprimand or censure,” he said.
He also said online newspapers and journalists do not fall under the jurisdiction of the Press Council Act.
Responding to a question from BNP lawmaker Joynal Abedin (Feni-2), the minister said Bangladesh ranked 152nd in the international press freedom index, while India ranked 157th and Pakistan 153rd.
In response to a question from Khilafat Majlis lawmaker Mohammed Abul Hasan (Sylhet-5), he said 39 of the 56 approved private television channels are currently operating in the country.
Of the 28 approved FM radio stations, 21 are currently broadcasting, the minister said, adding that there are currently 3,393 registered newspapers in the country.

Towhid Hridoy finished unbeaten on 350 for Bangladesh A against South Africa A in Potchefstroom on Wednesday, passing Tamim Iqbal's long-standing record for the highest first-class score by a Bangladeshi.

He went past Tamim's 334 on the final day of the four-day affair. Tamim set that mark for East Zone against Central Zone in the Bangladesh Cricket League at Mirpur in 2019.
Bangladesh A declared on 676 for eight, with Hridoy having faced 481 balls. Rejaur Rahman, who held up an end late in the innings, was 31 not out from 110 deliveries.

item.title: Minister Tuku hospitalised, condition stable
item.description:
Power, Energy, and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood Tuku is in stable condition after being admitted to hospital with fever, shortness of breath and a cough, hospital authorities said on Wednesday.
However, a medical board has advised him to remain in hospital for a few more days for further treatment and close monitoring.
The 76-year-old minister was taken to the emergency department of Ibrahim Cardiac Hospital and Research Institute in the capital at around 9:40pm on Tuesday after developing fever, shortness of breath and a cough.
Initial examinations found that he was experiencing shortness of breath and had low blood oxygen levels. He was subsequently admitted to the Coronary Care Unit (CCU).
In a statement, the hospital said doctors began treatment after reviewing the results of blood tests and a chest X-ray, which indicated pneumonia. A three-member medical board was immediately formed to oversee his treatment.
On Wednesday morning, a broader medical board comprising specialists from different disciplines was formed. His treatment is continuing in line with the board's recommendations, while further tests are being conducted as necessary.
Tuku has a history of diabetes and hypertension and recently underwent a procedure in Bangkok to have a stent placed in a coronary artery.
The medical board said he remains physically stable but will require a few more days in hospital for comprehensive treatment and close observation.

item.title: 5,000 US sailors arrive in Thailand after months at sea
item.description:
Around 5,000 US sailors and Marines arrived in Thailand on Wednesday for their first port call in nine months, after concerns over conditions on board sparked debate back home over President Donald Trump’s war with Iran.
The arrival of the USS Abraham Lincoln has made businesses in nearby Pattaya hopeful of a major windfall, but has also drawn renewed scrutiny of the resort town’s reputation as a hub for sex tourism.
The aircraft carrier docked in the port of Laem Chabang, south of Bangkok and a half-hour drive from Pattaya, for five days of rest and recreation after 286 days at sea, most recently in the Middle East.
“We’re all very excited, it should get quite lively,” said Anthony “AJ” Jones, a 60-year-old musician from New Zealand who performs every night at M’s Mojito beach bar in Pattaya.
A banner outside the bar reads: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”
“It’s been the talk of the town for the past few days... it will be a boon for businesses,” Jones told AFP, saying he was planning to perform some American classics to entertain the sailors.
With the world watching and an eye on the potential for trouble, Pattaya authorities have reportedly barred the sailors from the most notorious of the city’s streets, which are filled with hostess bars and semi-naked women.
The visitors will also be unable to engage in water sports, such as jet-skiing, and to take advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, according to Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches.
Authorities recently cracked down on sex workers in the city, Poramase told AFP, but insisted this was routine, denying it was linked to the Americans.
Security has also been stepped up.
“Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” Rear Admiral Robert Loughran, commander of the US Carrier Strike Group 3, said in a statement.
The Lincoln’s commanding officer, Captain Dan Keeler, added that its first port visit of the “historic deployment” would allow “our crew to enjoy this beautiful and historic country.”
The huge nuclear-powered carrier arrived early on Wednesday morning at Laem Chabang, with dozens of warplanes lined up on its flight deck, AFP reporters saw.
It was the first dry-land call since leaving California in November for duty in the South China Sea. The carrier was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran began in February.
Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on board -- including attempted suicides -- made headlines in the United States and provoked criticism of the ongoing conflict.
Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into conditions on board following reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises.
But Trump has dismissed the concerns.
“A small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life,” acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said in mid-August, blaming the media for “trying to paint our warriors as victims.”
The carrier was replaced in the Middle East by the USS George Washington, which had been in Japan.
That ship in turn will be relieved by the USS Theodore Roosevelt, which will sail from San Diego in the coming weeks, according to the private military association the US Naval Institute.
Pattaya comes to life at night and, in the hours before the US sailors arrived, the city appeared largely peaceful, with masseuses sitting idly outside their shops waiting for customers, and a few foreign tourists sunbathing on the beach.
One tailor shop posted a sign in its window offering clothes “Specially for US Navy -- Ready in 24 hours.”
“We’ll give them a special offer, good quality and a quick service -- 24 hours or even 12 hours,” said the owner, Islam.
“All of Pattaya is excited.”
The mayor said buses have been laid on to transport the sailors from the ship to Pattaya and back until the carrier departs on Sunday.
“Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them,” Poramase said in a video posted on Facebook.

item.title: Berger Paints Bangladesh, NDE Steel Structures sign two agreements
item.description:
Berger Paints Bangladesh Limited and NDE Steel Structures Limited have recently signed two separate agreements.
Under the first agreement, NDE Steel Structures Limited will undertake the steel structure works for key infrastructure at Berger Paints’ third manufacturing facility under construction at the National Special Economic Zone (NSEZ) in Mirsarai, Chittagong.
The project will further strengthen Berger’s manufacturing and supply chain capabilities while supporting its future business growth.
The new facility will significantly enhance Berger’s production capacity to meet the growing demand for paints and coatings in Bangladesh.
At the same time, the project is expected to create new employment opportunities, contribute to the development of local skills, and support the industrial and economic development of the Mirsarai region.
With its strategic location and world-class infrastructure, the National Special Economic Zone in Mirsarai is already emerging as one of the country’s key industrial destinations.
Berger’s new investment in the zone is expected to further contribute to the development of Bangladesh’s manufacturing and industrial sectors.
In addition, under the second agreement signed between the two companies, NDE Steel Structures Limited will exclusively use Berger Paints Bangladesh Limited’s products and solutions across its construction projects.
The agreement is expected to further strengthen the long-term business relationship between the two companies and expand the use of quality products and solutions across the industrial sector.
On behalf of Berger Paints Bangladesh Limited, the ceremony was graced by Mohsin Habib Chowdhury, chief executive officer & managing director; Abul Kasem Mohammad Sadeque Nawaj, chief business officer; Salahuddin Ahmed, chief marketing officer; Raquibul Alam, chief supply chain officer; Mahfuzul Haque, head of CAPEX and S&IM Procurement; and members of Berger's industrial sales team and the third factory project team were also present on the occasion.
Representing NDE Steel Structures Ltd, the attendees included Imran Mustafiz, managing director; Md Shamsuzzaman, chief executive officer; and Md Aminul Islam, deputy general manager, sales & marketing.
Commenting on the partnership, a senior official of Berger Paints Bangladesh Limited said: “We are delighted to partner with NDE Steel Structures Limited for this important project at our upcoming facility in Mirsarai. This investment reflects Berger’s long-standing commitment to innovation, manufacturing excellence, and sustainable growth in Bangladesh. We are confident that NDE’s expertise and capabilities will enable us to successfully complete the project on schedule while maintaining the highest standards of quality.”
A representative from NDE Steel Structures Limited said: “We are proud to be entrusted with the construction of the Water Base Production Building, Silo, and FG Warehouse for Berger Paints Bangladesh Limited’s Mirsarai facility. Drawing on our experience in industrial and steel structure projects, we are committed to completing the project safely, on schedule, and to the highest standards of quality and engineering excellence.”
Through this partnership, Berger Paints Bangladesh Limited and NDE Steel Structures Limited will continue to collaborate towards strengthening Bangladesh’s manufacturing infrastructure, advancing industrial development, and contributing to sustainable economic growth in the country.
